block.semiconductor-lab.refrigerator.not: A machine that runs on electricity and freezes water. A relative of refrigerators and air conditioners.
Compressor + 2 copper + 6 iron. 1 kW, 20 s. One ammonia water in the refrigerant slot (not used up); water bucket -> ice (the bucket returns).

In 1876 the German Linde built an ammonia compression refrigerating machine, letting breweries cool without winter ice. Linde later liquefied air to separate oxygen and nitrogen ([6-07] air separation).

The compressed, heated refrigerant is cooled outside into a liquid, then expanded suddenly through a narrow opening so it evaporates and draws heat from around it. It moves heat from cold to hot, so it is also called a heat pump. Semiconductor fab air conditioning and constant temperature ([12-12], [8-07]) work the same way.
block.semiconductor-lab.refrigerator.pla: Approximation: the real refrigerant is anhydrous ammonia (ammonia water here). Vanilla has no food spoilage, so there is no refrigerator function.
item.semiconductor-lab.vinegar.note1: A sour liquid you get by leaving alcohol open to the air.
item.semiconductor-lab.vinegar.note2: Put fermented wash (alcohol) in a fermentation crock and wait for 2. 2 vinegar + sodium hydroxide -> sodium acetate. About 5% acetic acid.
item.semiconductor-lab.vinegar.note3: Acetic acid bacteria from the air turn alcohol into acetic acid with oxygen: C2H5OH + O2 -> CH3COOH + H2O.
item.semiconductor-lab.vinegar.note4: In 1864 Pasteur showed that vinegar is made by acetic acid bacteria (Mycoderma aceti). Vinegar is humanity's first acid, thousands of years older than acetic acid from wood vinegar [2-23].
item.semiconductor-lab.vinegar.placehold: Approximation: acetic acid strength is fixed.
Alcohol warmed a little to cut down the germs in it. It will not turn to vinegar in the crock.
Warm fermented wash briefly on a campfire. The fermentation crock refuses it (no germs, so no vinegar). Compare with unheated wash.
A few minutes at about 60 C reduces the souring and spoiling germs without changing the taste. Boiling would drive off the alcohol and change the flavour.
In 1864 Pasteur showed this prevents the 'disease' that soured French wine. 'Pasteurize' on milk cartons is his name.
Approximation: the temperature is represented by a campfire.
item.semiconductor-lab.cane_juice.note1: Sweet juice pressed from sugar cane, cleared with lime.
item.semiconductor-lab.cane_juice.note2: 3 sugar cane + slaked lime + water bucket (bucket returned). Boil down on a campfire for 2 raw sugar.
item.semiconductor-lab.cane_juice.note3: Lime neutralizes the juice's acids and makes proteins and other cloudiness clump and settle (clarification).
item.semiconductor-lab.cane_juice.note4: Cane sugar has been made in India since around the start of the common era. Sanskrit 'sharkara' (grains of sand) is where 'sugar' comes from.
item.semiconductor-lab.cane_juice.placeh: Approximation: pressing and straining are skipped.
item.semiconductor-lab.beet_juice.note1: Sweet juice soaked out of sugar beet roots.
item.semiconductor-lab.beet_juice.note2: 4 beetroot + slaked lime + water bucket (bucket returned). Boil down on a campfire for 2 raw sugar.
item.semiconductor-lab.beet_juice.note3: Beet sugar is exactly the same sucrose, C12H22O11, as cane sugar.
item.semiconductor-lab.beet_juice.note4: Marggraf in Germany found sugar in beets in 1747, and Achard built the first beet sugar factory in 1801, so cold countries without cane could make sugar (it spread under Napoleon's Continental Blockade).
item.semiconductor-lab.beet_juice.placeh: Approximation: vanilla beetroot stands in for sugar beet (real sugar beet has a white root).
item.semiconductor-lab.raw_sugar.note1: Brown sugar from boiling down the juice. It still holds much colour and flavour.
item.semiconductor-lab.raw_sugar.note2: Boil juice down on a campfire for 2. 2 raw sugar + bone char + water bucket -> 2 white sugar.
item.semiconductor-lab.raw_sugar.note3: As the water boils off and it thickens, sucrose crystallizes. The surrounding molasses (brown liquid) carries the colour.
item.semiconductor-lab.raw_sugar.note4: Okinawan kokuto is cane juice simply boiled down like this.
item.semiconductor-lab.raw_sugar.placeho: Approximation: centrifuging off the molasses is skipped.
item.semiconductor-lab.bone_char.note1: Black grains from charred bone. They soak up colour very well.
item.semiconductor-lab.bone_char.note2: Char bones in a furnace (an approximation of heating without air). Used to turn raw sugar white (used up).
item.semiconductor-lab.bone_char.note3: Carbon coats the tiny pores of the bone's calcium phosphate, trapping the large colour molecules in them (adsorption).
item.semiconductor-lab.bone_char.note4: Used to decolourize sugar since the 19th century; activated carbon and ion exchange resins [2-17] are also used today.
item.semiconductor-lab.bone_char.placeho: Approximation: re-burning it for reuse is not modelled.
item.semiconductor-lab.tin_can.note1: An iron can with a thin coat of tin. It hardly rusts.
item.semiconductor-lab.tin_can.note2: Iron + tin -> 4. Add cooked meat or fish to make a sealed can.
item.semiconductor-lab.tin_can.note3: Tinplate is iron sheet dipped in molten tin. In 1810 Peter Durand in England patented keeping food in tin cans.
item.semiconductor-lab.tin_can.note4: For about 50 years after canning was invented there were no can openers; soldiers used bayonets or chisels ⚠️.
item.semiconductor-lab.sealed_can.note1: A filled, closed can. Not heated yet, so not canned food yet.
item.semiconductor-lab.sealed_can.note2: Heat it in a furnace or campfire to make canned food.
item.semiconductor-lab.sealed_can.note3: The key is to close it before heating: heat kills the germs inside, and the seal keeps new ones out. Heating first and closing afterwards lets germs in.
item.semiconductor-lab.sealed_can.note4: Appert did not know why it worked. The reason (germs) became clear about 50 years later through Pasteur's work in the 1860s.
item.semiconductor-lab.sealed_can.placeh: Approximation: real cans are boiled a long time in water (today at 120 °C under pressure). In the game you heat it in a furnace or campfire.
item.semiconductor-lab.canned_meat.note1: Food you can carry a long time. A little more filling than cooked meat.
item.semiconductor-lab.canned_meat.note2: Heat a sealed can in a furnace or campfire. Hunger 9 (cooked beef is 8).
item.semiconductor-lab.canned_meat.note3: In 1804-10, Nicolas Appert in France found that food packed into bottles, sealed and boiled kept for a long time, winning Napoleon's army prize. Tin cans came after.
item.semiconductor-lab.canned_meat.note4: Heating kills the germs, the seal keeps new ones out. Modern cans last for years.
item.semiconductor-lab.canned_meat.place: Approximation: the extra hunger is a game rule (real nutrition is about the same as cooked meat). No empty can is left. The game has no food spoilage.
A blue spray that protects crops like grapes from mould diseases.
Copper sulfate + slaked lime + water -> 4 (bucket returned). For now it is only crafted; there is no crop disease yet. ⚠ GHS: copper compounds harm aquatic life.

In 1885 Pierre-Marie-Alexis Millardet in France reported that it prevents downy mildew of grapes (a mould). Copper ions stop the spores from sprouting; the lime makes the copper stick to the leaves against rain and spares the leaves.
Bordeaux farmers painted the roadside vines with a blue mixture so passers-by would not steal the grapes - and only those vines escaped the disease. That was the clue.
Approximation: craft only. Crop disease and spraying to prevent it are not in the game (decision Q3-14 ②).
